lessons.title: Fungal Anatomy and Classification
lessons.body: Mushrooms are fungi, not plants. They lack chlorophyll and cannot make their own food. Instead, they digest dead organic matter like straw, sawdust, or cottonseed hulls. A mushroom has two main parts: the mycelium, a network of fine white threads that grows inside the substrate, and the fruiting body, which is the part you eat. The fruiting body includes the cap (pileus), gills (lamellae) under the cap, and stem (stipe). Some have a ring (annulus) or cup (volva) at the base. In Africa, the most commonly cultivated mushrooms are oyster (Pleurotus spp.) and button (Agaricus bisporus). Oyster mushrooms are easier for beginners because they grow on pasteurized straw and need less controlled conditions. Button mushrooms require compost and cooler temperatures. Classification: Kingdom Fungi, Phylum Basidiomycota (most edible mushrooms), Class Agaricomycetes, Order Agaricales. Oyster mushrooms belong to the genus Pleurotus, with species like P. ostreatus (grey oyster) and P. pulmonarius (phoenix oyster). Knowing the difference matters: oyster mushrooms have decurrent gills (running down the stem) and no volva, while deadly Amanita species have a volva and white spores. Always identify mushrooms correctly. For farming, buy certified spawn from reputable suppliers like those in Kenya, Nigeria, or South Africa. Never use wild spawn unless you are trained. The anatomy affects how you handle them: the mycelium is sensitive to heat and contamination, so keep your workspace clean. The fruiting body develops only when conditions are right, which we will cover later. In this lesson, focus on the basics: mycelium = vegetative part, fruiting body = reproductive part. Mushrooms reproduce via spores produced on gills. Each mushroom can release millions of spores, but in farming we propagate via mycelium on grain or sawdust. Understanding this prevents mistakes like exposing spawn to direct sunlight or mixing species.

lessons.title: Spore Germination and Mycelium Growth
lessons.body: Spores are like tiny seeds, but they are microscopic and produced in huge numbers. When a spore lands on a suitable substrate with moisture, it germinates and sends out a hypha (a single thread). Hyphae branch and fuse to form mycelium, the white fuzzy network you see on bread mould or on a colonized substrate. In mushroom farming, we usually skip spores and start with spawnâmycelium grown on grain or sawdust. Spawn is made by inoculating sterile grain with a pure culture. You can buy spawn from suppliers or make your own using tissue culture from a fresh mushroom. For beginners, buying spawn is safer. Spore germination requires: moisture (not soaking wet), nutrients (like sugars from grain), and a temperature around 24-28Â°C for oyster mushrooms. Darkness is not required but light can inhibit some species. Mycelium growth is the vegetative phase. It needs oxygen, so substrates must not be compacted. It also produces heat and CO2. In a bag, you will see condensation and the substrate turning white. Healthy mycelium is thick, white, and smells like mushrooms. Contaminated mycelium may be green (Trichoderma), black (Aspergillus), or slimy (bacteria). To grow mycelium successfully: pasteurize substrate (e.g., straw in hot water at 65-80Â°C for 1 hour), drain, cool, then mix with spawn at 5-10% of wet substrate weight. Pack into bags or bottles with breathable filters. Incubate in a dark room at 25Â°C. Oyster mycelium fully colonizes a 5 kg bag in 10-14 days. Button mushrooms take longer (3-4 weeks). During colonization, do not open bagsâcontamination risk. Check daily for temperature (should not exceed 30Â°C) and contaminants. If you see green, remove the bag immediately. Mycelium growth is the foundation: strong mycelium means good yields. Weak mycelium from old spawn or poor substrate will give few mushrooms. In Africa, many farmers use rice straw, wheat straw, or maize cobs. Chop to 2-5 cm pieces. Always use clean water. This stage is about patience and hygiene.

lessons.title: Fruiting Body Development
lessons.body: Once mycelium has fully colonized the substrate, it needs a trigger to form fruiting bodies. This is called pinning. Pins are tiny mushroom primordia that emerge from the mycelium. They look like small white dots or bumps. For oyster mushrooms, pins appear within 3-5 days after you introduce fresh air and light. The fruiting body develops in stages: pinhead, young mushroom, mature mushroom. The cap expands, gills become visible, and spores are released. In oyster mushrooms, the fruiting body is shelf-like with a short stem. In button mushrooms, it has a distinct cap and stem with gills that start pink then turn brown. Development requires: high humidity (85-95%), fresh air exchange (FAE), light (for direction, not photosynthesis), and a slight drop in temperature (e.g., from 25Â°C to 18-22Â°C for oysters). CO2 levels must be low; if too high, you get long stems and small caps (leggy mushrooms). For button mushrooms, a casing layer (peat moss + limestone) is added after colonization to induce fruiting. The casing must be kept moist. Fruiting bodies grow quickly: oyster mushrooms can double in size every 24 hours. Harvest before spores drop, usually when the cap edges are still slightly curled down. If you wait too long, spores drop and the mushroom becomes tough and messy. In Africa, many farmers grow oysters in simple humid rooms or even under trees with shade nets. You can use a bucket with holes or hanging bags. The key is to monitor daily: check humidity with a hygrometer (aim 85-90%), mist walls and floor (not directly on mushrooms), and open vents for FAE. If pins turn brown and dry, humidity is too low. If stems are long and thin, increase FAE. Fruiting happens in flushes: you get a group of mushrooms, then a rest period, then another flush. Oyster mushrooms typically give 3-4 flushes over 2-3 months. Proper development ensures good market quality. Handle mushrooms gentlyâthey bruise easily.

lessons.title: Substrate Colonization
lessons.body: Substrate is the material mushrooms grow on. It provides nutrients and a place for mycelium to spread. Common substrates in Africa: rice straw, wheat straw, maize stover, cottonseed hulls, sawdust (hardwood, not softwood), coffee husks, banana leaves, and water hyacinth. Each has different properties. Straw is cheap and widely available. Sawdust needs supplementation with bran (10-20%) for better yields. Cottonseed hulls are excellent but may be expensive. Before use, substrate must be pasteurized or sterilized to kill competitors. Pasteurization: soak chopped straw in hot water at 65-80Â°C for 1-2 hours. You can use a drum with a fire underneath. Sterilization: for sawdust, use a pressure cooker or steam for 2-3 hours at 121Â°C. After heating, drain excess water. The substrate should be at field capacity: squeeze a handful, and only a few drops come out. Moisture content around 65-70%. Then cool to below 30Â°C before adding spawn. Mix spawn thoroughly at 5-10% of wet weight. For a 10 kg bag, use 500 g to 1 kg spawn. Pack into bags or bottles. Make sure bags have filter patches for gas exchange. Colonization: place in a dark room at 24-28Â°C. Do not stack bags too high; heat builds up. Check daily. White mycelium should spread from the spawn grains. After 10-14 days for oysters, the bag should be completely white. If you see any green, black, or pink patches, remove that bag. A sour smell means bacterial contamination. Successful colonization is when the substrate is firm and white. At this point, the bag is ready for fruiting. In Africa, many farmers use the 'bottle technique' for small-scale: fill plastic bottles with substrate, sterilize, inoculate, and colonize. This reduces contamination. Another method is the 'bag log' used for shiitake. For oysters, the simplest is the 'hanging bag' method: colonized bags are hung and slit to allow mushrooms to grow out. Always keep records: date of spawning, temperature, and observations. Colonization is the silent phase; it determines your yield. If contamination occurs, clean the area with 70% alcohol or bleach solution. Never reuse contaminated substrate.

lessons.title: Environmental Triggers for Fruiting
lessons.body: Mushrooms fruit when environmental conditions change. The main triggers are: temperature drop, fresh air exchange (FAE), light, and humidity. For oyster mushrooms, a drop from 25Â°C to 18-22Â°C signals fruiting. In nature, this happens after rain or at night. In your grow room, you can use a fan or open vents to lower temperature and CO2. CO2 levels should be below 800 ppm for oysters. High CO2 causes long stems and small caps. Light: mushrooms need light to know which way to grow, but not for photosynthesis. A 12-hour light cycle from a fluorescent bulb or indirect sunlight is enough. Direct sunlight will dry and kill pins. Humidity: keep relative humidity at 85-95%. Use a hygrometer. Mist the floor and walls, not the mushrooms. If you mist mushrooms directly, they can get bacterial blotch. FAE: exchange air 4-6 times per day. You can use a small fan on a timer or manually open vents. For button mushrooms, the triggers are different: a drop to 16-18Â°C, high humidity, and a casing layer. The casing layer (peat moss + limestone) is applied after colonization and kept moist. It provides a reservoir of moisture and bacteria that stimulate fruiting. In Africa, many farmers use simple evaporative cooling: hang wet sacks on windows, or use a fan blowing over a water tray. In dry areas, you may need a humidifier. In humid areas, you may need a dehumidifier to prevent mould. Monitor daily: check temperature (min-max thermometer), humidity, and CO2 (if you can afford a meter). Adjust by opening/closing vents, turning on fans, or misting. Fruiting usually starts 3-7 days after triggering. Pins appear as small white dots. Do not disturb them. If pins dry out, they abort. If you see pins, maintain conditions. Harvest within 2-4 days. After harvest, clean up debris and let the substrate rest for 7-10 days before the next flush. The environmental triggers are the same for most gourmet mushrooms, but check species-specific needs. For example, shiitake needs a cold shock and soaking. Oysters are more forgiving. Always keep a log of what works.

lessons.title: Harvesting Stages and Indicators
lessons.body: Harvesting at the right time gives you the best quality and shelf life. For oyster mushrooms, harvest when the cap edges are still slightly curled down and before they flatten or turn upward. The gills should be clean and white to cream. If you wait until spores drop, the mushrooms become messy and less attractive. Spores can also cause allergies. For button mushrooms, harvest when the cap is closed (buttons) or slightly open (flats). The veil should be intact for buttons. If the veil breaks and gills are exposed, they are still edible but have shorter shelf life. For shiitake, harvest when the cap is 70-80% open and the edges are still curled in. For milky mushrooms, harvest when caps are convex. Indicators to watch: size (varies by species; oysters 5-15 cm across), colour (should be uniform), firmness (firm, not spongy), and moisture (dry surface but not cracked). Harvest by twisting and pulling gently, or cutting with a clean knife at the base. Do not pull out the substrate. For oyster mushrooms, you can harvest the whole cluster at once. Use clean hands and tools. After harvest, place mushrooms in a clean container. Do not wash them; just brush off debris. Store in a paper bag or perforated plastic bag in a cool place (4-8Â°C). They last 5-7 days. For market, grade by size and appearance. In Africa, fresh mushrooms sell quickly in urban markets, hotels, and restaurants. You can also dry them for longer storage. Harvest in the morning when it's cool. After harvesting, remove any remaining stems and debris from the substrate. This reduces contamination. Then let the substrate rest for 7-10 days. During rest, keep humidity lower (70-80%) and stop misting. After rest, you can trigger another flush by repeating the environmental triggers. Typically, you get 3-4 flushes. The first flush is the largest. Record your yields: weight per bag, number of mushrooms, and any issues. This helps you improve. Always handle mushrooms gentlyâthey bruise easily. Use a sharp knife to cut the stem cleanly. If you see any mould on harvested mushrooms, discard them. Proper harvesting ensures repeat customers and good income.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Mushroom Biology & Life Cycle for African Growers

This practical reference distils the biology you need to run a commercial mushroom operation in Africa. It is written for the grower, not the mycologist: every section links back to yield, contamination control, cost, and market timing. Use it alongside the six lessons in this module as a field manual you can pin to the wall of your growing house.

In most African markets, the highest-margin species for small and medium enterprises are oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus ostreatus, P. pulmonarius, P. eryngii), shiitake (Lentinula edodes) in cooler highland zones, and button mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus) where cold-chain and compost infrastructure exist. The biology below applies broadly; species-specific notes are flagged.

1. Anatomy and Classification â What Matters Commercially

Mushrooms are fungi in the phylum Basidiomycota (most cultivated species) or Ascomycota (e.g. morels, some medicinal fungi). The parts you manage are the mycelium (the vegetative network that eats substrate), the primordia (pinheads), and the fruiting body (the marketable product). The fruiting body has a cap, gills or pores, a stem, and often a ring or volva. For grading and pricing, cap size, stem length, and colour uniformity are the traits buyers pay for.

Classification drives your production plan: Pleurotus species are primary decomposers that grow on pasteurised agricultural waste â a competitive advantage in Africa where cottonseed hulls, maize cobs, rice straw, banana leaves, and sawdust are cheap. Agaricus requires composted substrate and tighter climate control, a higher-capex route. Know your species before you build.

2. Spore Germination and Mycelium Growth

Spores germinate into hyphae that fuse to form dikaryotic mycelium. In practice, growers skip spores and buy spawn â grain or sawdust colonised by proven mycelium. Spawn quality is the single largest determinant of first-flush yield. Store spawn at 2â6 Â°C, out of direct sun, and use within the supplier's window.

Mycelium grows radially, extending 2â10 mm per day under good conditions. It secretes enzymes that break down cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. This is why substrate particle size and moisture matter: too fine and it compacts anaerobically; too coarse and colonisation is slow and contamination wins the race.

3. Substrate Colonisation â The Make-or-Break Phase

Colonisation is a race between your mycelium and competitors (green mould Trichoderma, bacteria, and insect pests). Win it with three levers: clean spawn, correct moisture (65â75% for most Pleurotus substrates), and pasteurisation or sterilisation. In African smallholder systems, hot-water pasteurisation at 60â70 Â°C for 60â90 minutes, or lime (calcium hydroxide) soaking, are low-cost and effective. Steam sterilisation is preferable for sawdust and supplemented substrates.

Maintain substrate temperature at 22â28 Â°C for Pleurotus; Lentinula prefers 20â24 Â°C. Keep the colonisation room dark or dimly lit, with passive or filtered air exchange. Full colonisation typically takes 14â28 days depending on species, substrate, and spawn rate (use 5â10% spawn by wet weight for reliable results).

Table 1. Key cultivation parameters by species (typical African smallâmedium enterprise conditions)
ParameterPleurotus ostreatus (oyster)Lentinula edodes (shiitake)Agaricus bisporus (button)
SubstrateStraw, cottonseed hulls, sawdust, maize cobsHardwood sawdust + bran, sterilisedComposted horse/poultry manure + straw
Colonisation temp.22â28 Â°C20â24 Â°C22â25 Â°C (compost)
Fruiting temp.15â22 Â°C12â20 Â°C14â18 Â°C

Light500â1,000 lux, 12 h/day500â1,000 lux, 12 h/dayLow, indirect
Days to first flush21â3535â6028â42 after casing
Typical BE (fresh wt / dry substrate)60â100%50â80%70â100%

Sources: Oei, P. Mushroom Cultivation: Appropriate Technology for Developing Countries (Agromisa/CTA); FAO agricultural training materials; Zied et al. (2016), Edible and Medicinal Mushrooms.

4. Fruiting Body Development and Environmental Triggers

When mycelium has fully colonised the substrate, it needs a trigger to shift from vegetative growth to reproduction. The classic triggers are:

  • Temperature drop (cold shock) â e.g. from 26 Â°C to 18 Â°C for oyster mushrooms.
  • Fresh air exchange â lowering COâ below 800â1,000 ppm.
  • Light â 500â1,000 lux for 12 hours a day; essential for normal cap and stem development.
  • Humidity â 85â92% RH at the pinning surface.
  • Mechanical disturbance â some growers scratch or "ruffle" the casing or bag surface.

Pinheads appear within 3â7 days of triggering. Over the next 3â5 days they enlarge into harvestable fruiting bodies. Poor triggers produce long stems, small caps, and low market value â a direct revenue loss.

5. Harvesting Stages and Indicators

Harvest timing determines shelf life, price, and the size of the next flush. For Pleurotus, harvest when the cap margin is still slightly inrolled and before spores are released (spore drop causes allergies and reduces shelf life). For Agaricus, harvest at the "closed veil" stage for premium fresh market, or "open veil" for processing. For shiitake, harvest when the cap is 70â80% expanded and the edge is still slightly curled.

Twist and pull, or cut with a clean knife at the base. Handle with clean gloves; bruising is a major post-harvest loss. Cool to 4 Â°C within 2 hours of harvest where cold chain exists; otherwise sell within 24 hours and use evaporative cooling or shade to extend shelf life.

Table 2. Harvest indicators and post-harvest targets
SpeciesHarvest indicatorTarget shelf lifePost-harvest action
Oyster (Pleurotus)Cap margin inrolled, no spore drop5â7 days at 4 Â°CCool fast, pack in perforated liners
ShiitakeCap 70â80% expanded, edge curled10â14 days at 4 Â°CDry or cool; high value fresh
Button (Agaricus)Veil closed (premium) or just open7â10 days at 2â4 Â°CPre-cool, no washing before sale
Milky (Calocybe)Cap still convex, firm2â3 days ambientSell same day in local markets

Sources: FAO post-harvest handling guidance; Oei, P. (Agromisa); Zied et al. (2016).

â  SAFETY WARNING â Do not eat unidentified mushrooms.

Africa has many wild fungi, some of which are deadly (e.g. Amanita phalloides and related species). Never consume a wild mushroom unless it has been identified by a qualified mycologist. Never sell wild-collected mushrooms to the public. Always keep spawn, cooked mushrooms, and cleaning chemicals separate from wild specimens. Grow only from certified spawn of known edible species. Wash hands and tools after handling substrate and before handling food.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Buy certified spawn from a reputable supplier; record batch and date.
  2. Pasteurise or sterilise substrate â 60â70 Â°C for 60â90 min, or lime soak, or steam.
  3. Target 65â75% substrate moisture; squeeze test: a few drops, not a stream.
  4. Use 5â10% spawn by wet weight; mix thoroughly and pack evenly.
  5. Colonise in the dark at 22â28 Â°C; keep the room clean and pest-free.
  6. Trigger fruiting with cold shock, fresh air, light (500â1,000 lux), and 85â92% RH.
  7. Harvest before spore drop; handle with clean gloves; cool fast.
  8. Track yield per bag and per flush; cull contaminated bags immediately and away from the grow room.

Further Reading (free, official)

  • FAO â Mushroom Cultivation and related agricultural training resources: fao.org (search "mushroom cultivation").
  • Agromisa / CTA â Mushroom Cultivation: Appropriate Technology for Developing Countries (Agrodok 40): agromisa.org.
  • International Centre for Mushroom Science (ICMS): icms.org.
  • Wageningen University & Research â mushroom research and open-access publications: wur.nl.
  • African Union / NEPAD â agribusiness and horticulture value-chain resources: nepad.org.

Business note: In African markets, consistent quality and reliable supply win contracts with supermarkets, hotels, and restaurants. Biology is the lever: master colonisation and fruiting triggers, and you control yield, shelf life, and therefore margin. Keep records per bag, per flush, and per customer â this is how a small mushroom house becomes a bankable agribusiness.

quiz.q: What are the two main parts of a mushroom?
quiz.explanation: Mycelium is the vegetative network; fruiting body is the reproductive structure we eat.

quiz.q: Which genus do oyster mushrooms belong to?
quiz.explanation: Oyster mushrooms are in the genus Pleurotus, such as P. ostreatus.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between oyster and button mushrooms in cultivation?
options: A) Oyster needs compost, button needs straw
B) Oyster grows on straw, button needs compost and cooler temps
C) Oyster needs casing, button does not
D) Oyster is poisonous, button is edible
quiz.explanation: Oyster mushrooms grow well on pasteurized straw; button mushrooms require compost and cooler conditions.

quiz.q: What is spawn?
options: B) Mycelium grown on grain or sawdust
quiz.explanation: Spawn is mycelium propagated on a carrier like grain, used to inoculate substrate.

quiz.q: What temperature range is ideal for oyster mycelium growth?
quiz.explanation: Oyster mycelium grows best at 24-28Â°C; higher temperatures risk contamination.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of fruiting in oyster mushrooms?
quiz.explanation: Pins are tiny mushroom primordia that emerge from colonized mycelium.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of pasteurizing substrate?
options: D) To make it easier to pack
quiz.explanation: Pasteurization kills harmful bacteria, fungi, and pests that compete with mushroom mycelium.

quiz.q: What moisture content should substrate be at before spawning?
quiz.explanation: Substrate should be at field capacity, around 65-70% moisture, so a squeeze yields a few drops.

quiz.q: What is a common sign of contamination during colonization?
quiz.explanation: Green patches usually indicate Trichoderma, a common contaminant; remove the bag immediately.

quiz.q: What environmental trigger is essential for fruiting?
quiz.explanation: FAE reduces CO2 and provides oxygen, which is necessary for pinning and fruiting body development.

quiz.q: What relative humidity is ideal for fruiting oysters?
quiz.explanation: High humidity (85-95%) prevents pins from drying out and supports proper development.

quiz.q: What happens if CO2 levels are too high during fruiting?
options: B) Mushrooms develop long stems and small caps
quiz.explanation: High CO2 causes leggy mushrooms with long stems and small caps due to insufficient FAE.

quiz.q: When should you harvest oyster mushrooms?
options: A) When cap edges are curled down
C) When cap is flat and spores are releasing
quiz.explanation: Harvest when cap edges are still slightly curled down for best quality and shelf life.

quiz.q: What is a casing layer used for?
quiz.explanation: Button mushrooms require a casing layer (peat moss + limestone) to induce fruiting.

quiz.q: How many flushes can you typically get from oyster mushrooms?
quiz.explanation: Oyster mushrooms usually produce 3-4 flushes over 2-3 months with proper care.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store harvested mushrooms?
options: B) In a paper bag in a cool place
D) In a sealed plastic bag at room temperature
quiz.explanation: Paper bags allow some breathability and prevent moisture buildup; cool temperatures extend shelf life.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see green mould on a colonizing bag?
options: C) Remove and discard the bag
D) Open it for fresh air
quiz.explanation: Green mould is a contaminant; remove the bag to prevent spread to healthy bags.

quiz.q: What is the role of light in mushroom fruiting?
quiz.explanation: Light helps mushrooms orient their growth, but they do not photosynthesize.

quiz.q: What is the ideal spawn rate for oyster mushrooms?
quiz.explanation: Using 5-10% spawn ensures rapid colonization and reduces contamination risk.

quiz.q: Which substrate is commonly used in Africa for oyster mushrooms?
quiz.explanation: Rice straw is widely available and works well for oyster mushrooms after pasteurization.

quiz.q: What is the first step in substrate preparation?
quiz.explanation: Chopping increases surface area; pasteurization kills competitors before spawning.

quiz.q: What does a sour smell from a colonizing bag indicate?
quiz.explanation: A sour smell is a sign of bacterial contamination; remove the bag.

quiz.q: How long does it take for oyster mycelium to fully colonize a 5 kg bag?
quiz.explanation: Under optimal conditions (24-28Â°C), oyster mycelium colonizes in about 10-14 days.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a filter patch on a mushroom bag?
quiz.explanation: Filter patches allow oxygen in and CO2 out while blocking contaminants.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to harvest mushrooms?
quiz.explanation: Harvest in the morning when it's cool to maintain freshness and reduce stress on the mushrooms.

quiz.q: What should you do after harvesting a flush?
options: B) Remove debris and let rest
quiz.explanation: Cleaning and resting the substrate for 7-10 days allows recovery for the next flush.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a common substrate in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Pine sawdust contains resins that inhibit mushroom growth; hardwood sawdust is preferred.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for fruiting oyster mushrooms?
quiz.explanation: A drop to 18-22Â°C triggers fruiting for most oyster strains.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of leggy mushrooms?
quiz.explanation: High CO2 from poor FAE causes long stems and small caps.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to harvest a mushroom cluster?
options: A) Pull hard from the base
B) Twist and pull gently or cut with a knife
quiz.explanation: Gentle twisting or cutting at the base prevents damage to the substrate and mycelium.
